stages.name: Limits of HDI
stages.title: Limits of HDI
stages.sub: Understand why HDI is an incomplete measure of development and what else can be used instead.

steps.q: Two countries have identical HDI scores. One has clean rivers, free elections and strong human rights; the other has heavy pollution, a one-party state and no free press. Does HDI tell them apart?
steps.right: No, HDI looks the same for both
steps.wrong: Yes, HDI is lower for the polluted one
steps.hint: HDI is built only from income, health and education data. Where would pollution or political freedom show up in that?

steps.q: You already know HDI combines income, health and education by giving each dimension the same weight in the average. Is there any economic reason that all three must matter exactly equally to every country?
steps.right: No, that equal split is just a choice someone made
steps.wrong: Yes, the three dimensions are naturally equal in importance
steps.hint: A poor country recovering from a health crisis and a rich country with weak schools might value each dimension very differently. Does the formula reflect that?

steps.q: You now know HDI leaves out things like pollution and freedom, and even the way it weights income, health and education is a debatable choice. If you fixed the weighting, would HDI then capture everything about a country's development?
steps.right: No, it would still miss things like the environment and freedom
steps.wrong: Yes, fixing the weights would make it complete
steps.hint: Weighting and omission are two separate gaps. Does closing one gap close the other?

steps.q: Since no single combined score can cover income, health, education, inequality, the environment and freedom all at once, how many measures would you need to build a fuller picture of development?
steps.right: Several different measures, each covering different gaps
steps.hint: Think about how many separate gaps you have just found. Could one more index close every one of them at once?
